analysis.one_liner: Limits how much of a 401(k) can be locked into company stock and guarantees workers control and information.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared a Senate committee on July 26, 2002 with 14 cosponsors, but was never brought to a Senate floor vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Written after the Enron collapse, when employees were locked out of their 401(k) accounts during a changeover while executives sold stock, this bill would have rewritten the rules for retirement plans that invest in the employer's own shares. Workers would get the right to sell company stock from their accounts — immediately for their own contributions, within three years for employer matches — plans would have to offer at least three other investment options, and statements each quarter would warn anyone with more than 20 percent of their account in employer stock. It also required 30 days' notice before any lockdown period that freezes a worker's account, removed the shield that usually protects employers from lawsuits during lockdowns, imposed personal liability on company insiders who knowingly take part in or hide a breach of fiduciary duty, barred companies from forcing workers to sign away their right to sue over pensions, and created a Pension Participant Advocacy office inside the Labor Department.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers in 401(k)-style plans that hold employer stock — the people whose retirement savings can be wiped out in a single company's collapse or trapped during an account blackout.

how_it_helps.text: Workers would have the immediate right to move their own contributions out of employer stock, and after no more than three years of service to move employer contributions, into any other option the plan offers [S3].

Plans would have to offer at least three investment choices besides company stock, and accounts more than 20 percent in employer stock would carry an explicit 'overinvested' warning on quarterly statements [S3].
Plans would have to give 30 days' notice before any lockdown freezing access to accounts, and during a lockdown the sponsor would lose the usual safe harbor from fiduciary liability [S3].

Company officers, directors, and plan accountants would be personally liable for knowingly participating in or concealing a breach of fiduciary duty, and participants could sue to recover losses and profits [S3].
The right to sue over pension claims could no longer be waived by pre-dispute agreements; arbitration would be allowed only if entered into knowingly and voluntarily after a dispute arises [S3].

Plans with more than 100 participants would be held in trust by a joint board including trustees elected by participants, fiduciaries would have to carry insurance against breaches, and a new Office of Pension Participant Advocacy in the Labor Department would help participants pursue claims [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers that sponsor 401(k) plans — especially companies that use their own stock as the vehicle for matching contributions — would bear the compliance costs, fiduciary insurance, new trustee structures, and the risk of lawsuits; the financial services firms that administer plans and give investment advice would also face new obligations and recordkeeping costs.

drawbacks.text: The diversification and disclosure rules carry real compliance costs, and small and mid-sized employers without large benefits departments would feel them most [S3].

Employers that maintain a qualifying traditional pension covering at least 90 percent of the same employees would be exempt from the prohibition on pushing both matches and worker contributions into company stock, so the strictest rules would fall only on companies that offer nothing but the 401(k) [S3].

The bill shields plan sponsors from liability for investment advice if they designate a 'qualified investment adviser,' a carve-out that benefits the advisory industry and could give sponsors a way to shift responsibility for bad advice [S3].

Mandatory fiduciary insurance for plans with more than 100 participants adds a recurring premium cost that would ultimately be borne by employers and, to some degree, workers through reduced contributions or benefits [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protections — the right to get out of company stock, advance notice before account lockdowns, honest statements, and liability for insiders who hide breaches — respond directly to harms workers have already suffered, and those benefits plausibly outweigh the compliance costs, which are largely administrative. The main design weaknesses are the defined-benefit exemption, which softens the mandate for companies that also run traditional pensions, and the investment-adviser carve-out, which narrows accountability. On balance it is a consumer-protection bill with modestly burdensome but reasonable compliance costs, and it never got a chance to be tested or amended on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate health and labor committee approved it on July 26, 2002 and placed it on the Senate calendar, but no senator ever got to vote on it before that Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

narrative.text: Senator Kennedy introduced the bill on March 6, 2002 with 14 original cosponsors, 13 Democrats and 1 Republican [S1] [S5].
It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which considered and marked it up on March 20 and ordered it reported favorably with an amendment on March 21 [S6].
The committee formally reported the bill on July 26, 2002 with a substitute amendment, written Report 107-226, and minority views were filed [S6].
The same day, the bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 525 — meaning it was ready and waiting for a floor vote [S6] [S4].
No further action was ever taken: the bill never received a floor vote, was never sent to the House, and died when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that use their own stock as the default vehicle for retirement savings, and plan sponsors and fiduciaries generally, are better off because the bill died — they avoided the diversification mandates, lockdown notice rules, personal insider liability, fiduciary insurance, and participant-elected trustees it would have imposed. Workers who lost savings concentrated in employer stock got nothing from this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies and plan sponsors that avoided the new rules

sides.party_line_note: 13 of the 14 cosponsors were Democrats, the committee report carried Republican minority views, and no floor vote ever took place to reveal where the full Senate stood.

industries.industry: Employers sponsoring 401(k) plans with company stock
industries.note: The bill bars plans from pushing both employer contributions and worker deferrals into employer stock (unless the employer also runs a qualifying traditional pension), forces diversification rights, and strips liability protections during account lockdowns — all of which stop companies from using worker retirement money as a captive source of capital. For workers, the same rules are the protection: they prevent savings from being trapped in one company's shares.

Registered advisers gain a defined, protected role: sponsors who designate a 'qualified investment adviser' are shielded from liability for that advice, locking in advisers as the channel for 401(k) investment guidance. But the bill also imposes fiduciary duties, accurate-disclosure requirements with up to $1,000-a-day fines, and insurance mandates on the people and firms advising participants.

Fiduciaries of plans covering more than 100 participants would have to carry insurance against breaches of duty, creating a new market for coverage whose purpose is to make workers whole if a plan fails them.
